title: Excalidraw: AI and Human Whiteboarding Partnership - Christopher Chedeau

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Christopher Chedeau opens by warning that the first half of his talk is non-AI setup. He recounts Excalidraw's origin: in January 2020, procrastinating on Facebook performance reviews, he tried to use Zibl for blog illustrations, found it down, and reimplemented it with rough.js in CodeSandbox. A Twitter post got 200 likes, signaling demand. He mentions Anthropic recently demoed an AI agent building Excalidraw's requested table layout feature (no PR yet). When COVID sent everyone home, Excalidraw became a whiteboarding tool by accident. Chedeau contrasts it with competitors that mapped physical constraints one-to-one: fixed-size canvases, traced letters, pixel-by-pixel erasing, freehand shapes, no copy-paste. Excalidraw's virtual-native approach—infinite canvas, text boxes, select-delete, shape selection, copy-paste—was a breakthrough. He draws an analogy: current AI integrations resemble early online whiteboards—sprinkling AI on existing paradigms yields poor results. He walks through three AI attempts. First, Gorecam's ML model converted sketches to realistic images, but users don't draw realistic images. Second, direct LLM diagram generation produced unrecognizable output. Third, LLMs reliably generate Mermaid JS syntax, and a contributor built an Excalidraw backend for Mermaid, enabling prompt-to-diagram with editable output—AI provides ~90%, humans refine. He envisions future iterative AI modification rather than one-shot generation. Additional integrations include automatic document naming (LLMs generate names from content after users stop working), illustration generation (in closed alpha, to be open-sourced soon), and a call for audience-built browser-based logo background removal. He concludes with three lessons: we're in a physical-to-virtual moment for AI-native interactions; resist shipping models that don't truly help users; and LLMs love structure—find domain-specific languages for LLMs to target, then convert to your system without AI.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Excalidraw originated as a procrastination-driven reimplementation of Zibl using rough.js, went viral on Twitter, and accidentally became a whiteboarding tool during COVID.
Virtual-native features (infinite canvas, keyboard text, select-delete, shapes, copy-paste) beat competitors that mapped physical whiteboard constraints one-to-one.
Current AI integrations parallel early online whiteboards: sprinkling AI on existing paradigms produces poor results; we must discover AI-native interactions.
Just because an AI model exists doesn't mean it belongs in your product—image generation failed because Excalidraw users draw diagrams, not realistic images.
LLMs reliably generate Mermaid JS syntax; a custom Excalidraw backend for Mermaid enabled successful prompt-to-diagram with editable output.
The human-AI partnership means AI generates ~90% as editable Excalidraw components; users refine layout, colors, and positions; future work aims for iterative refinement.
LLMs love structure—representing your problem domain as a domain-specific language lets LLMs target it reliably, then you convert output to your system without AI.
Ship only AI models that genuinely help users accomplish their goals; resist the urge to ship every available model.
Additional integrations include automatic document naming from content and illustration generation (in closed alpha, open-sourcing soon).

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Structure Warning
sections.summary: Chedeau introduces himself as Excalidraw's creator and warns that the first half of the talk is non-AI setup, with AI content in the second half.

sections.title: Origin Story of Excalidraw
sections.summary: In January 2020, procrastinating on Facebook performance reviews, Chedeau tried to use Zibl for blog illustrations. It was down, so he reimplemented it with rough.js in CodeSandbox. A Twitter post got 200 likes, launching Excalidraw. He notes he'd use coding agents today and mentions Anthropic demoed an AI agent building Excalidraw's table layout (no PR yet).

sections.title: COVID and the Whiteboarding Problem
sections.summary: Three months later, COVID sent everyone home. People needed virtual whiteboarding; Excalidraw, built for blog illustrations, was accidentally a good fit.

sections.title: Physical vs. Virtual Whiteboard Comparison
sections.summary: Competitors mapped physical constraints one-to-one: fixed-size canvases, traced letters, pixel-by-pixel erasing, freehand shapes, no copy-paste. Excalidraw's virtual-native features—infinite canvas, text boxes, select-delete, shape tools, copy-paste—were breakthroughs.

sections.title: AI Integration Analogy and Overview
sections.summary: Chedeau draws an analogy: current AI integrations resemble early online whiteboards—sprinkling AI on existing paradigms yields poor results because nobody has experience yet. The conference helps share lessons to improve this.

sections.title: AI Attempt 1: Image Generation (Rejected)
sections.summary: Gorecam (FAL AI) found an ML model converting Excalidraw sketches to realistic images. It worked technically, but users don't draw realistic images on Excalidraw. Key lesson: just because a model exists doesn't mean it belongs in your product.

sections.title: AI Attempt 2: Direct LLM Diagram Generation (Failed)
sections.summary: LLMs asked to generate Excalidraw diagrams directly produced unrecognizable output. Chedeau notes a Gemini demo shown yesterday can output Excalidraw files, making his talk already outdated.

sections.title: AI Attempt 3: Mermaid JS and Human-AI Partnership
sections.summary: LLMs reliably generate Mermaid JS syntax describing diagrams as text. A contributor built an Excalidraw backend for Mermaid, enabling prompt-to-diagram. Output is a real, editable Excalidraw component—users adjust layout, colors, and positions, embodying the human-AI partnership where AI provides ~90% and humans refine.

sections.title: Future Vision and Additional AI Integrations
sections.summary: Chedeau envisions future iterative AI modification rather than one-shot generation. He shares additional integrations: automatic document naming (LLMs suggest names after users stop working, solving the untitled-file problem), and illustration generation for infographics (in closed alpha, to be open-sourced soon). He challenges the audience to build a browser-based logo background-removal model for Excalidraw.

sections.title: Conclusions and Key Lessons
sections.summary: Three conclusions: (1) We're in a physical-to-virtual whiteboard moment for AI-native design interactions—need to discover what AI-native looks like. (2) Resist shipping random models; only ship ones that genuinely help users. (3) LLMs love structure—represent your problem as a domain-specific language, let LLMs target it, then convert to your system without AI. He closes by introducing the next speaker, Steve, who will talk about TLDRdraw.
